what.text: Ketamine is a general anesthetic given by injection into a vein or a muscle. The FDA label for Ketalar says it is used as the only anesthetic for procedures that do not need muscle relaxation, to start anesthesia before other anesthetics, and alongside other anesthetics.
How it acts, according to the FDA label

items.text: Ketamine blocks the NMDA receptor, a receptor for the brain chemical glutamate. Its main breakdown product, norketamine, acts on the same receptor more weakly.
It produces a 'dissociative' anesthetic state: strong pain relief, with throat reflexes and muscle tone kept. It raises blood pressure, heart rate and cardiac output, and it widens the airways.

Ketamine is a 50:50 mix of two mirror-image forms. The S form, esketamine, is sold on its own as Spravato nasal spray, which is approved for depression. Spravato's label says it is not approved as an anesthetic.
The liver breaks ketamine down mainly through the enzymes CYP2B6 and CYP3A4. After an injection into a vein, the first phase, which matches the anesthetic effect, has a half-life of 10 to 15 minutes.

research.text: Ketamine's approval rests on its use as an anesthetic. Its use for depression is off-label. Trials of that use started with a 7-person study in 2000 and now include a 403-person comparison with ECT. Each is listed below as it was run.

research.title: First placebo-controlled test in depression (Biol Psychiatry 2000)

facts.v: Berman RM, Cappiello A, Anand A, et al. Biol Psychiatry 2000;47(4):351-4
randomized, double-blind; each person had a ketamine day and a saline day
7 people with major depression completed the study
a single infusion of ketamine 0.5 mg/kg or saline into a vein
2 test days; ratings for 72 hours after each
25-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale

research.found: Depression scores fell by an average of 14 points within 72 hours after ketamine, and by 0 points after saline. The authors called it the first placebo-controlled trial of an NMDA blocker in depression.

src.label: Berman et al., Biological Psychiatry, PubMed

research.title: Treatment-resistant depression at NIMH (Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006)

facts.v: Zarate CA Jr, Singh JB, Carlson PJ, et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006;63(8):856-64
randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind crossover, 2004 to 2005
18 adults with treatment-resistant major depression
one infusion of ketamine 0.5 mg/kg or placebo into a vein, a week apart
ratings up to 7 days after each infusion
21-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale

research.found: Scores improved more after ketamine than placebo from 110 minutes after the infusion, and the gap lasted through the week. The day after ketamine, 71% met response and 29% met remission criteria; 35% still met response criteria a week later.

src.label: Zarate et al., Archives of General Psychiatry, PubMed

research.title: Ketamine vs midazolam as an active placebo (Am J Psychiatry 2013)

facts.v: Murrough JW, Iosifescu DV, Chang LC, et al. Am J Psychiatry 2013;170(10):1134-42
two-site, parallel-arm, randomized, double-blind; midazolam (an anesthetic) as the control so both groups felt a drug effect
73 adults with treatment-resistant major depression, randomized 2:1
a single infusion of ketamine or midazolam into a vein
primary result at 24 hours
Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS)

research.found: At 24 hours, MADRS scores were 7.95 points lower with ketamine than midazolam. Response rates were 64% and 28%. The authors said more data on how long the effect lasts and on safety were needed before clinical use.

src.label: Murrough et al., American Journal of Psychiatry, PubMed

research.title: Ketamine vs ECT, ELEKT-D (N Engl J Med 2023)

facts.v: Anand A, Mathew SJ, Sanacora G, et al. N Engl J Med 2023;388(25):2315-25
open-label, randomized, noninferiority, 5 sites (NCT03113968)
403 adults with treatment-resistant depression without psychosis, referred for ECT; 195 got ketamine and 170 got ECT
ketamine 0.5 mg/kg into a vein over 40 minutes twice a week, or ECT three times a week
3-week treatment phase; responders followed for 6 months
response (at least a 50% fall in depression score); memory tests; quality of life

research.found: 55.4% responded on ketamine and 41.2% on ECT, which met the test for ketamine being no worse than ECT. ECT was linked to a drop in memory recall and to muscle and bone side effects; ketamine was linked to dissociation.

src.label: Anand et al., New England Journal of Medicine, PubMed

research.meta: New Zealand, Australia, Singapore, Taiwan · 2024 · Phase 2 randomized trial
research.title: Extended-release ketamine tablets, R-107 (Nat Med 2024)

facts.v: Glue P, Loo C, Fam J, et al. Nat Med 2024;30(7):2004-9
5-day open-label phase, then responders randomized, double-blind, to 4 doses or placebo
231 adults with treatment-resistant depression entered; 168 responders were randomized
R-107, an investigational extended-release ketamine tablet, 30 to 180 mg twice a week, or placebo; most doses were taken at home
12 weeks of double-blind treatment
change in MADRS at 13 weeks

research.found: At 13 weeks the 180 mg group scored 6.1 points better than placebo on MADRS. Relapse was 70.6% on placebo and 42.9% on 180 mg. The authors reported no blood pressure changes and little sedation or dissociation. R-107 is not approved in the US.

src.label: Glue et al., Nature Medicine, PubMed

research.text: The label reports that, in published animal studies, anesthetic drugs that block NMDA receptors increased nerve-cell death in the developing brain and caused lasting learning problems when given for more than 3 hours. In pregnant rats and rabbits, ketamine caused skeletal defects and more lost pregnancies. These findings are in animals.

us.text: Ketamine is FDA approved, by prescription, as Ketalar (1970), an anesthetic. It is a Schedule III controlled substance. No ketamine product is FDA approved for depression; that use is off-label. Compounded ketamine is not FDA approved. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: FDA's Drugs@FDA data show NDA 016812 approved February 19, 1970, as a new molecular entity, as an injection. The label lists only anesthetic uses.
the label says Ketalar contains ketamine, a Schedule III controlled substance. DEA's rules list 'Ketamine, its salts, isomers, and salts of isomers' in Schedule III, at 21 CFR 1308.13(c)(7).

ketamine infusions, lozenges and nasal sprays for depression are off-label. The only ketamine-type drug FDA has approved for depression is esketamine nasal spray (Spravato), given in certified health care settings under a REMS.

the Ketalar label says ketamine 'is associated with hepatobiliary dysfunction (most often a cholestatic pattern), with recurrent use (e.g., misuse/abuse or medically supervised unapproved indications).' It asks for baseline liver tests and regular checks in anyone given repeated doses.

FDA's list of compounding risk alerts includes, on October 10, 2023, 'FDA warns patients and health care providers about potential risks associated with compounded ketamine products, including oral formulations, for the treatment of psychiatric disorders', and, on February 16, 2022, 'FDA alerts health care professionals of potential risks associated with compounded ketamine nasal spray'. FDA now links both alerts only to archived copies, which could not be opened for this page.
FDA says compounded drugs are not FDA approved, and that FDA does not verify their safety, effectiveness or quality before they are marketed.

src.label: FDA, Compounding and the FDA: Q&A

us.text: Compounded ketamine (lozenges, tablets, nasal sprays) is not FDA approved. Ketamine for depression is off-label.

world.lead: Ketamine is an approved medicine, used in anesthesia, in the US, Canada, the UK, the EU and Australia. It is a controlled drug in the US (Schedule III), Canada (Schedule I), the UK (Class B) and Australia (Schedule 8). It is not named on the WADA Prohibited List.

countries.status: Approved medicine (Ketalar 1970, anesthesia). Prescription-only, Schedule III. Depression use is off-label.
Approved medicine. Ketalar and generic ketamine injections are listed as marketed. The database lists ketamine under Schedule I of the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act.

after.text: In January 2026 the UK's Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs (ACMD) published an updated review of ketamine harms. It advised that ketamine stay Class B, raised concern about growing high-dose use, and called for a patient registry to track off-label prescribing of ketamine and esketamine.

after.title: Sport
after.text: Ketamine is not named anywhere on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List. Class S7 (narcotics, prohibited in competition) lists only these named opioids: buprenorphine, dextromoramide, diamorphine (heroin), fentanyl and its derivatives, hydromorphone, methadone, morphine, nicomorphine, oxycodone, oxymorphone, pentazocine, pethidine and tramadol. Ketamine is not among them, and it is not named in S6 (stimulants) or any other class. The 2027 List, in force January 1, 2027, and the 2027 Monitoring Program do not name it either.

side.text: The label lists emergence reactions (vivid dreams, hallucinations, confusion on waking) and raised blood pressure and pulse as the most common side effects. Serious risks include breathing problems, liver and bile-duct injury and bladder damage with repeated use, abuse and dependence.

items.text: about 12% of patients had confusion or agitation while waking up, usually lasting a few hours. Reactions range from dream-like states to vivid imagery, hallucinations and delirium.

blood pressure, heart rate and cardiac output often rise; falls in blood pressure and heart rate, abnormal rhythms and heart failure have also been seen. Ketamine must not be used where a big rise in blood pressure would be a serious hazard.

breathing can slow or stop with an overdose or a fast injection. Combined with opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol or other sedatives, it can cause profound sedation, breathing problems, coma and death.
repeated use has been linked to liver injury, narrowing and blockage of bile ducts and sclerosing cholangitis, which may reverse after stopping.
long-term use or abuse has been linked to cystitis, a smaller bladder, narrowed ureters and kidney swelling (hydronephrosis), sometimes needing emergency surgery.
a rise in pressure inside the skull has been reported.

the label says ketamine can be abused. Repeated high-dose misuse may affect memory and attention. Tolerance, physical dependence and withdrawal (craving, fatigue, poor appetite, anxiety) have been reported with heavy long-term use.
the label warns that anesthetics like ketamine given for more than 3 hours, from late pregnancy to about age 3, may affect brain development, based mainly on animal studies.
in the ELEKT-D trial, ketamine was linked to dissociation. In the 2024 tablet trial, the most common side effects were headache, dizziness and anxiety.

unconfirmed: FDA's October 2023 alert on compounded ketamine (including oral forms) and its February 2022 alert on compounded ketamine nasal spray are now linked from FDA's Compounding Risk Alerts page only as archived copies on web.archive.org, which could not be reached. Only their titles and dates, from FDA's live list, are cited; their full text was not read.
MHRA's product database did not load without a browser; the UK licence number comes from EMA's list of nationally authorised ketamine products, which lists it for Northern Ireland.
Whether any EU member state authorises a ketamine product for depression was not checked.
surprises: The Ketalar label now warns of liver and bile-duct injury with recurrent use, naming 'medically supervised unapproved indications' alongside misuse; repeated off-label dosing for depression falls under that wording.
Health Canada's database lists ketamine under Schedule I of the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act, the same schedule as opioids such as heroin, while the US places it in Schedule III.
FDA has moved its compounded-ketamine safety alerts off its live website; its own list now links to archived copies.
